See more Published 12 April 2026 9:00am BST Ukrainians have more than a decade of familiarity with Russia being a dishonest peace broker. After the 2014-15 Donbas war began, Russian-aligned Donetsk People’s Republic militias occupied Ilovaisk and Ukrainian forces embarked on an intensive campaign to liberate the city. Because of command structure miscues and war materiel limitations, Ukrainian troops in Ilovaisk were swiftly encircled.Vladimir Putin and Alexander Zakharchenko, the Donetsk People’s Republic chief, responded by proposing a safe humanitarian corridor for Ukrainian forces to leave the city. Due to Russia’s history of using humanitarian passageways as offensive traps, Kyiv rejected Putin’s offer. The result was a brutal massacre of almost 400 Ukrainian soldiers.This is the context in which we should see the Orthodox Easter ceasefire in Ukraine announced by Putin. The Kremlin has decreed that Russian forces cease hostilities from 4pm on Saturday to end-of-day on Sunday. As Volodymyr Zelensky, the Ukrainian president, previously called for a joint cessation of energy facility attacks over Easter, Kyiv will welcome this ceasefire proposal.Although Russia has gone from ignoring Zelensky’s pleas for peace to embracing a ceasefire, Putin’s gesture is not a magnanimous one: the Kremlin has a long history of violating ceasefires it rhetorically supports, and does not view this truce as a stepping stone towards de-escalating the Ukraine war.Russia’s duplicitous track record towards ceasefires dates back to the August 2008 Georgian War. Immediately after agreeing to retreat to pre-war positions under a French-led peace formula, Russia established 25 new military checkpoints and entrenched its occupation of large swathes of Georgian territory.During its military intervention in Syria, Russia habitually accused American-backed rebel forces of ceasefire violations and carried out brutal air strikes against Syrian civilians.Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine has caused the bitter memory of the Donbas war betrayal to be constantly relived. In January 2023, Patriarch Kirill, the head of the Russian Orthodox Church, implored Russian and Ukrainian forces to agree to a 36-hour truce.Citing his autonomy from the Russian defence ministry’s command structure, Yevgeny Prigozhin, the Wagner Group chief, flouted the ceasefire and used the de-escalation to consolidate control over the Donetsk battleground of Soledar. During last year’s Easter ceasefire, Russia claimed that it wanted to halt fighting to test Ukraine’s willingness to pursue peace, but proceeded to launch artillery fire across the front lines.More of the same double-speak is to be expected from Russia this weekend. Even though Kyiv’s long-range drone strikes are wreaking havoc on Russian military logistics, and Starlink cutoffs are enabling Ukrainian gains on the southern front, Putin’s goal of subjugating Ukraine remains unchanged.Kremlin press secretary Dmitry Peskov’s praise of the two-week Iran truce and calls for new American-led Ukraine talks are almost certainly a red herring to buy time.
